newsitem.title: TAIWAN: S.Africa plan to recognise China stuns Taiwan.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa plan to recognise China stuns Taiwan.

text.p: News that South Africa had decided on Wednesday to sever ties with Taiwan and recognise communist China took the Nationalist-ruled island by surprise, with officials scrambling to decide how to react.
Officials entering the Foreign Ministry late on Wednesday rushed without comment past reporters who were barred from entering the building and told to await a statement.

State radio quoted Vice Premier Hsu Li-teh as saying the situation was "not that serious" but left unclear whether he was reacting to news of the planned diplomatic switch or to Pretoria's intent to announce it.

Senior officials were attending a private banquet in Taipei when Foreign Minister John Chang took a telephone call, suddenly took on a serious look, spoke briefly with Premier Lien Chan and hastily departed, state radio said.
Diplomatic sources said Taipei had only a few hours' notice of the shock decision before South African President Nelson Mandela formally revealed it in Johannesburg.
Mandela told a news conference at his Johannesburg home that the process of recognising Beijing would be a gradual one that he hoped could be completed within a year.
"A permanent continuation of diplomatic recognition of the Republic of China on (the island of) Taiwan is inconsistent with South Africa's role in international affairs," Mandela said.
South Africa was the biggest of Taiwan's 30 diplomatic allies.

Officials of Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government, regarded by the communist mainland as a renegade regime since a civil war split them in 1949, had taken succour from Mandela's recent remarks that it would be "immoral" to abandon Taiwan.
Until Wednesday, Mandela had resisted intense pressure from Beijing to drop Taipei and recognise the People's Republic of China, saying he wanted good relations with "both Chinas".
Mandela's two China formulation is heresy to Beijing, which reserves a right to use force to bring Taiwan under its rule.
South Africa's Taipei ambassador, Johannes Viljoen, told Reuters by telephone that he only learned of the decision during his supper some two hours before it was announced.
He said he sincerely hoped Pretoria could maintain economic relations with Taipei and that Taiwan would not take reprisals against South Africa in the form of reduced cooperation.

"Of course they are a very important trading partner of South Africa, our sixth largest, and also an important source of assistance," he said. "We sincerely hope the projects they have going in South Africa would continue."
Increasingly isolated diplomatically by China, Taiwan has tried to use its economic muscle to keep ties with the states that still recognise it instead of Beijing.

Beijing has obliged all countries with which it establishes diplomatic ties to drop Taiwan, though it allows its diplomatic friends to maintain economic and other unofficial ties with the industrial juggernaut.
